title: NAT and Port Forwarding
oneLiner: How a whole office shares one public IP address, why the internet can't reach your devices unless you forward a port, and why port forwarding often fails behind carrier-grade NAT.
keyTakeaway: NAT rewrites addresses at the edge of a network. Port address translation lets many private devices share one public address by giving each outbound connection its own public port in a NAT table. Inbound connections that nobody inside started have no table row, so they're dropped unless a port forwarding rule says where they go.
explanation:
There aren't enough IPv4 addresses for every device, so homes and companies use private addresses inside (10.x, 172.16 to 172.31, 192.168.x) and share a few public ones at the edge. NAT (Network Address Translation) is the router rewriting addresses as packets cross it. The common form, PAT (Port Address Translation, also called NAT overload or masquerading), rewrites the source address and, when necessary, the source port of every outbound connection, and records the mapping in a NAT table. When a reply comes back to the public address and port, the table says which inside device and port it belongs to.

A side effect is that nothing on the internet can start a connection to an inside device: an unsolicited packet matches no table row and is dropped. Port forwarding (sometimes called a destination NAT rule) is a manual exception: "anything arriving on public port 8443 goes to 192.168.1.50 port 443". It's how a camera or a server is published, and it's also how many networks get breached, because that device is now reachable by every scanner on the internet. Remote Desktop and industrial protocols should never be forwarded; use a VPN instead.

Two details explain a lot of confusing support calls. Many internet providers now put customers behind carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT, the 100.64.0.0/10 range), a second NAT you can't configure, so your port forwards never see the traffic. And NAT is not a firewall: it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic by accident, but it doesn't filter outbound traffic or inspect anything.
